title: Redis Pipeline Batching Under Latency Budgets: Command Coalescing, RTT Amortization, and the Flush Boundary Problem
description: How Redis pipelining amortizes RTT across batched commands, where flush boundaries create latency cliffs, and how to tune batch sizing in Go services.
linkedin_post:
Redis pipelining is frequently misunderstood as a simple throughput trick. It's actually a latency budget tool — and where you place the flush boundary determines whether it helps or creates a latency cliff.

In a new article, I work through the full mechanics:

→ RTT amortization arithmetic: why 10 serial GET calls at 500 µs VPC RTT costs 5 ms, and how pipelining collapses that to ~600 µs
→ The flush boundary problem: too-early flush defeats the RTT gain, too-late flush makes P99 latency proportional to accumulation window length, not command cost
→ Server-side head-of-line blocking: expensive commands inside a pipeline stall cheap ones — command class segmentation matters
→ TxPipelined vs Pipelined: different atomicity contracts, different error semantics, different failure modes under partial results
→ A channel-based batcher goroutine in Go with dual-trigger flush (batch size + timer) for coalescing across goroutines without shared mutable state
→ A decision function for batch sizing derived from your latency budget and per-command server time — not an arbitrary constant

The key production insight: batch size and flush interval are configuration parameters that belong under observability. Instrument pending batch size at flush time as a histogram. If your p50 batch size is 2, you are not getting the gains the architecture promises.
